🧭 Executive Summary
This document defines the complete roadmap for the stabilization, observability, configuration, and reintegration of DawnTrader — transforming the refactored V1 system into a production-grade, self-monitoring, and autonomy-ready architecture.

📋 Summary of Phases (Overview)
Phase 5C — Observability Setup
Goal: Implement full-stack observability for metrics, health, and logs.

Integrate system-wide metrics collection (TradingEngine, Guardrails, LATTI, Queue, Telemetry).

Implement /api/metrics, /api/health, and /api/logs/recent endpoints.

Build frontend Observability Dashboard (uptime, queue depth, latency charts).

Add JSON-structured logging with correlation IDs and timestamps.

Define 5 key SLOs: signal latency, order latency, portfolio staleness, queue depth, and event-loop lag.

Introduce color-coded alerts for SLO violations.

Validate with 48-hour runtime test and metrics reporting.

Phase 6 — Config Registry & Runtime Governance
Goal: Centralize configuration management and runtime safety.

Create Config Registry (config_registry table + REST API).

Register all critical runtime flags: ENABLE_LATTI, CLE_ENABLED, MAX_POSITIONS, KILL_SWITCH%, etc.

Implement GET /api/config and PUT /api/config endpoints (role-gated).

Add runtime change tracking (ConfigAuditService).

Build Config UI panel with editable toggles (admin-only).

Integrate registry into startup logic; remove hard-coded flags.

Validate with runtime flag toggles and persistence verification.

Phase 7 — Paper Mode Stability Test
Goal: Verify 24/7 runtime stability and trade coherence under simulated conditions.

Run 48-hour paper trading stress test.

Validate zero memory leaks and sub-5s portfolio lag.

Monitor queue saturation and trade lifecycle consistency.

Add runtime_metrics.csv export per hour.

Detect and auto-handle stuck trades or missed heartbeats.

Generate continuous anomaly reports and verify recovery logic.

Pass/fail criteria: no crashes, <1% SLO violations.

Phase 7.5 — Automated Tests & CI Enhancements
Goal: Reinforce stability via automation.

Create Jest + Playwright test suites for backend and UI.

Add CI/CD workflow (GitHub Actions or Replit Deploy Hooks).

Automate linting, type checks, build validation, and E2E tests.

Integrate code coverage thresholds (>85%).

Schedule nightly builds and health tests.

Generate /audit/phase7.5-test-results.md with pass/fail logs.

Phase 8 — Controlled Autonomy Re-Enable
Goal: Reactivate LATTI and Orchestrator autonomy safely.

Gradual reactivation: Reasoning → CLE → Ethics.

Enforce two-person approval rule for live mode autonomy.

Restore AdaptiveGuardrails and MotivationEngine modules.

Validate Lottie’s learning adjustments in paper mode.

Implement hard throttles (max 3 adaptive changes / 24h).

Create LATTI Insights dashboard (reasoning logs, motive states).

Verify alignment: no rogue actions or unsafe signals.

Phase 9 — Code Hardening & Legacy Purge
Goal: Achieve final production readiness.

Audit for deprecated imports, unused files, and duplicate code.

Replace temporary debug logs with structured telemetry.

Run npm audit, fix vulnerabilities.

Implement read-only API key enforcement and final security sweep.

Tag stable release: v2.0.0-Alpha.

Phase 5C – Observability Setup (Full Implementation)
🎯 Objective
Establish a comprehensive observability layer enabling real-time monitoring of the trading engine, telemetry, LATTI, and queue systems.

🧩 Components
Metrics Service (server/services/metrics-service.ts)

Calculates SLO adherence.

Emits JSON metrics payloads via WebSocket (metrics_update).

Health Endpoint

/api/metrics: returns system SLOs and subsystem performance.

Frontend Observability Dashboard

/monitoring route.

Displays color-coded cards (green/yellow/red) per metric.

Auto-refresh every 15 seconds.

Structured Logging

Replace console.log with logger.info() / logger.error().

Include trace_id, symbol, mode, and timestamp.

Alert Engine

Emits warnings when any metric breaches defined thresholds.

Integrated into health monitor.

🧪 Validation

Capture metrics every minute.

Validate metrics accuracy ±2%.

Verify zero log gaps >5 seconds.

🎯 Objective

Runtime Hooks

2. Backend Implementation
Create: server/services/config-service.ts

import db from "../db";
import { logger } from "../utils/logger";

export class ConfigService {
  static async getAll() {
    const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT key, value, type, updated_at, updated_by FROM config_registry ORDER BY key");
    return rows;
  }

  static async get(key: string) {
    const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT * FROM config_registry WHERE key=$1", [key]);
    return rows[0];
  }

  static async update(key: string, value: any, type: string, user: string) {
    await db.query(
      `INSERT INTO config_registry (key, value, type, updated_by)
       VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4)
       ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE
       SET value=EXCLUDED.value, type=EXCLUDED.type, updated_at=NOW(), updated_by=EXCLUDED.updated_by`,
      [key, value, type, user]
    );
    logger.info("Config updated", { key, user });
  }
}

import React, { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { Card, CardContent } from "@/components/ui/card";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";

export default function SystemConfig() {
  const [configs, setConfigs] = useState([]);

  async function loadConfigs() {
    const res = await fetch("/api/config");
    setConfigs(await res.json());
  }

  async function updateConfig(key, value, type) {
    await fetch("/api/config", {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ key, value, type })
    });
    await loadConfigs();
  }

  useEffect(() => { loadConfigs(); }, []);

  return (
    <div className="p-6 space-y-4">
      {configs.map(cfg => (
        <Card key={cfg.key} className="shadow-md">
          <CardContent className="flex justify-between items-center">
            <div>
              <p className="font-semibold">{cfg.key}</p>
              <p className="text-xs text-gray-500">{cfg.type}</p>
            </div>
            <Button onClick={() => updateConfig(cfg.key, cfg.value, cfg.type)}>Update</Button>
          </CardContent>
        </Card>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

That message always means React hooks are being called conditionally or inside a loop — the number of hooks changes between renders, which React strictly forbids.

✅ How to fix it cleanly
1️⃣ Open
client/src/pages/system-config.tsx

You’ll find something like:

{configs.map((cfg, i) => {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(cfg.value);   // ❌ hook inside map

This must be refactored so that all hooks are called at the top level, not inside .map().

2️⃣ Replace that pattern with a subcomponent
Create a nested child component that manages its own state:

function ConfigRow({ cfg, onUpdate }) {
  const [value, setValue] = React.useState(cfg.value);

  const handleChange = async (e) => {
    const newVal = e.target.value;
    setValue(newVal);
    await fetch("/api/config", {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ key: cfg.key, value: newVal, type: cfg.type }),
    });
    onUpdate?.();
  };

  return (
    <div className="flex justify-between items-center p-2 border-b">
      <span>{cfg.key}</span>
      <input
        value={value}
        onChange={handleChange}
        className="border rounded px-2 py-1 w-40 text-right"
      />
    </div>
  );
}
Then update your main render:

export default function SystemConfigPage() {
  const [configs, setConfigs] = React.useState([]);

  React.useEffect(() => {
    fetch("/api/config")
      .then(res => res.json())
      .then(setConfigs)
      .catch(console.error);
  }, []);

  if (!configs.length) return <div className="p-4">Loading configuration...</div>;

  return (
    <div className="p-6">
      {configs.map(cfg => (
        <ConfigRow key={cfg.key} cfg={cfg} onUpdate={() => {}} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}
✅ Each ConfigRow runs its own useState, but the parent no longer violates the Rules of Hooks.

guardrails_v2 (the new table) only has:

const riskPerTrade = (balance * portfolioRiskPerTradePct / 100).toFixed(2);

If you have $10,000 balance and set 2% risk per trade in the Guardrails tab

This is the intended behavior - percentage-based risk that adapts to your portfolio size, which is why Phase 41F-L.E2E-PURGE removed the old fixed-dollar approach.

⚙️ Now, about the engines — paper vs. live
Here’s the simple picture:

Concept	What it Does	Data Source	Execution Type
Paper (simulation)	Simulates trading with fake money. It listens to real Kraken market data to make decisions and record simulated trades.	✅ Real market data from Kraken	❌ No real trades – it just “pretends” to buy/sell
Live (real trading)	Places real buy/sell orders on your actual Kraken account using your API key and executes trades with real money.	✅ Real market data from Kraken	✅ Real trades via Kraken API
Right now, you have only the first half — the paper trading engine.

It does connect to Kraken’s data feeds — so it’s looking at real prices, volume, and market activity — but when it “buys” or “sells,” it only updates your local database (simulated P&L, positions, etc.). It does not send any orders to Kraken.

So when you switch the mode from “paper” to “live” right now, you’re basically just telling the same simulation code:

It’s still the same simulation engine under the hood.

It will still use the same risk logic, guardrails, and behavioral variables.

await krakenService.placeOrder(symbol, quantity, price)
using your Kraken API credentials.

The trade results will come from Kraken’s confirmation — not from simulated logic.

Subject: Scanner tuning: fast loop for Top-100, safe throttling, and ready-to-buy polling

Hey team — a few tuning requests to get us the best of both worlds (breadth + speed) without bumping rate limits:

1) Fast lane for Top-100 (every ~60s) without breaking the budget
Goal: Re-evaluate “Top-100 by 24h volume” roughly once per minute.

Constraint: Keep the global average ≤ ~1.5 req/sec (your logs show ~1.4–1.5 req/sec today with 60 pairs every ~40–45s).

Two acceptable ways to do it:

Option A — WebSocket-first (preferred if our Kraken WS is stable):

Subscribe tickers for the Top-100 via WS and drive re-evaluation primarily off WS updates.

REST is only for misses/backfill (e.g., gaps, first touch, or fields not on WS).

This gives us ~“continuous” freshness on the Top-100 at near-zero extra REST cost.

Option B — REST-only compromise (if we must):

Refresh Top-80 per 60s (80/min ≈ 1.33 req/sec).

The next 20 of the Top-100 can be folded into the rolling batches so the whole Top-100 still gets covered ~every minute-ish while staying ≤ 1.5 req/sec overall.

If you want a clean round figure: Top-100 every 90s also works (100/90 ≈ 1.11 req/sec), leaving more headroom for the long tail.

Please implement Option A if possible; otherwise use Option B (80/min).

2) Rolling batches for the long tail (full universe)
Keep the rolling batch architecture you just restored (👏).

New target cadence (if REST-only): ~25 seconds per sub-cycle, ~35 pairs per sub-cycle → ~1.4 req/sec sustained.

(If you prefer round numbers: 30s × 45 pairs → ≈ 1.5 req/sec. Either is fine; pick the one that stabilizes best in practice.)

That keeps us safely under limits while rotating the remaining ~1,300–1,400 pairs in ~10–15 minutes.

3) Tiering rule (who gets scanned when)
Tier A (Top-100 by 24h volume): Fast lane above (WS preferred or 80/min REST).

Tier B (everything else): Rolling batches as above.

Important: This is priority, not exclusion. Tier B still rotates fully; Tier A just gets touched much more often.

4) Shorter sub-cycle timing and larger batch sizes
You asked about 20–30s sub-cycles and 70–80 pairs per sub-cycle.

Pure REST at 25s × 70 pairs would be ≈ 2.8 req/sec — too high.

If we switch the Top-100 to WS, we can keep REST ≈1.4–1.5 req/sec for Tier B and still achieve very quick responsiveness overall.

tl;dr: To raise batch size or shorten intervals, move Top-100 to WS; keep REST budget around ~1.4–1.5 req/sec.

5) Ready-to-Buy watch loop (extra calls?)
Yes, candidates in Ready-to-Buy need tighter monitoring to catch entry conditions.

Plan:

🧩 Step 2. Patch the safeNumber() utility to include origin tracing

export function safeNumber(value: any, origin = "unknown") {
  if (value == null || isNaN(value)) {
    console.warn(`[SafeNumber:WARN] Invalid number in ${origin}`, { value });
    return 0; // or '--' if you prefer UI placeholder
  }
  try {
    return Number(value);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(`[SafeNumber:ERR] Exception in ${origin}`, err);
    return 0;
  }
}

export function safeLocale(value: any, origin = "unknown") {
  try {
    const n = safeNumber(value, origin);
    return n.toLocaleString();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(`[SafeLocale:ERR] Failed in ${origin}`, err);
    return "--";
  }
}

🧩 Step 3. Wrap each dashboard widget with componentDidCatch tracing

class WidgetErrorBoundary extends React.Component<any, any> {
  constructor(props: any) {
    super(props);
    this.state = { hasError: false, error: null };
  }

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error: any) {
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: any, info: any) {
    console.error("[WidgetBoundary:Caught]", this.props.name, error, info.componentStack);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return (
        <div style={{ padding: "1em", border: "1px solid red" }}>
          <b>Component Error:</b> {this.props.name}
          <pre>{String(this.state.error?.message)}</pre>
        </div>
      );
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

Excellent — this was a huge step forward, and now we can make sense of the full picture.
Let’s break it down clearly so you know what Replit did, why the error happened, how it was fixed, and why it’s now stable.

🧩 What Was Really Happening
The Root Cause
All along, the white screen (and later, the “Component Error”) was caused by one rogue line of code in filter-health-widget.tsx:

diagnostics.pairsScanned.toLocaleString()
That line assumed that diagnostics.pairsScanned was always defined and numeric —
but in reality, sometimes the backend wasn’t returning a value at all, meaning pairsScanned was undefined.

So when React tried to run .toLocaleString() on undefined, it crashed the entire dashboard render tree.

That was the single trigger for all the blank screen symptoms we’ve been seeing.

🧠 Why It Was Hard to Catch Earlier
The problem didn’t appear in the widgets Replit had already instrumented (like Portfolio Value, Earnings, or Averages).
FilterHealthWidget hadn’t been wrapped with any of the new safety utilities (safeNumber, DataProbe, etc.).

So the earlier diagnostics didn’t catch this one because:

It was an un-instrumented widget.

The crash happened before React Query’s “safe” fallback values had a chance to kick in.

That’s why the dashboard crashed after ~30–40 seconds — once the diagnostics data refreshed and sent back an undefined count.

🧩 How Replit Found It (Brilliantly)
Replit added a global trap override for Number.prototype.toLocaleString —
basically a “spy” that logs every time that function is called with bad data.

It looked like this:

Number.prototype.toLocaleString = function (...args) {
  if (this === undefined || this === null || isNaN(this)) {
    console.error('[GlobalTrap] Invalid toLocaleString call', this, new Error().stack);
  }
  return originalToLocaleString.apply(this, args);
};
That instantly showed the exact file and line where .toLocaleString() was being misused:
filter-health-widget.tsx line 111.

That’s what made the bug visible — a perfect debugging move.

🧩 The Fix (Two-Layered)
✅ 1. Frontend fix (safety wrapper)
They replaced:

{diagnostics.pairsScanned.toLocaleString()}
with:

{safeNumber(diagnostics.pairsScanned, {
  origin: 'FilterHealthWidget.pairsScanned',
  useLocaleString: true,
  decimals: 0
})}
safeNumber() ensures:

If the value is undefined, it logs a [SafeNumber:WARN] message in the console (for future debugging),

Returns a placeholder like '--' instead of crashing,

Uses proper locale formatting when the number exists.

✅ 2. Backend fix (data normalization)
They also added a guarantee in the API response itself:

const response = {
  pairsScanned: Number(scanResult.universe_count ?? 0),
  eligiblePairs: Number(scanResult.eligible_count ?? 0),
  failurePercent: Number(failurePercent ?? 0),
  ...
};
That way, even if Kraken or the analytics job returns null or undefined,
the backend automatically converts it to 0.

So now, the frontend will never again receive undefined numeric values.

🧩 3. Defensive Enhancements Added
They wrapped the GlobalTrap in a dev-only guard,
so it only runs during development (not in production).
This ensures debugging tools don’t slow down the live version.

They left DataProbes active, which means:
if any future component gets bad data, you’ll see something like:

[DataProbe:PortfolioWidget] totalValue is undefined
but the dashboard won’t crash.

They confirmed backend refactors were rolled back, so no conflicting architecture changes remain.

🧩 Why It’s Stable Now
Now, every layer — backend and frontend — defends against this kind of crash:

Layer	Protection	Effect
Backend	Normalizes undefined → 0	No undefined numeric fields in API
Frontend (Widgets)	safeNumber()	Catches any missing numbers before rendering
React Query	placeholderData: previousData	Keeps old data until new data arrives
Error Boundaries	Per-widget isolation	One widget crash doesn’t blank the whole page
GlobalTrap	Dev-only sentinel	Detects future .toLocaleString() misuse instantly
Together, these prevent both silent crashes and data integrity errors.

🧩 TL;DR – What You Can Tell Stakeholders
The “white screen” and “Component Error” issues were caused by a single missing null-check in the Filter Health widget.
The team fixed it by adding defensive number formatting (safeNumber) and backend normalization to ensure all API responses return numeric values.
The dashboard is now fully stable and crash-proofed at both the frontend and backend layers.

🧭 Why We’re Moving to the Three-Mode Architecture
Right now, the system runs all data-flow and scanning logic through one shared execution path, with runtime flags distinguishing paper vs. live trading.
Over time this single-path setup has led to several problems:

Cross-contamination of data and API calls between modes (e.g., passive data feeding into live filters).

Mode-specific logic patched in multiple places, creating maintenance risk.

Difficulty verifying whether paper and live executions are truly behaving independently.

Challenges simulating live trading conditions without risking interference with production balances.

To solve these permanently, we’ll split the system into three discrete but coordinated modes, each with its own responsibilities, life cycle, and API touchpoints — all orchestrated through a clean Mode Registry / Orchestrator layer.

🧩 Phase 1 – Three-Mode Architecture Audit (Starting Now)
Objective: identify every component, service, or data path that behaves differently (or should behave differently) depending on mode.

Deliverables:

Mode Dependency Map – enumerate every place in the codebase that references mode, simulation, paper, or live.

API Contract Audit – verify which endpoints should serve each mode, what parameters or schema differences exist, and whether normalization is consistent.

State and Storage Audit – catalog where state is shared across modes (watchlists, signals, trades, portfolios) and where it should be isolated.

Guardrail Integration Audit – confirm kill-switch, loss-limits, and guardrails logic applies correctly and independently to each mode.

Logging & Telemetry Plan – design mode-scoped logging so we can view performance and risk metrics per mode.

This audit should end with a concise architectural brief outlining what must be separated or refactored to support the three-mode system cleanly.

⚙️ Phase 2 – Implementation of Three Execution Engines
Once the audit is complete and validated, the next development cycle will build three self-contained but interoperable engines:

Passive Learning Mode

Runs continuously even when trading is off.

Streams live Kraken data for pattern recognition and model training (Latti’s observation engine).

No trades executed; minimal lightweight API calls.

Paper Execution Mode

Uses the current paper-sim engine as its foundation.

Performs full batch scanning, filtering, strategy evaluation, deduplication, expiration, and simulated trade execution.

Tracks portfolio performance in simulation tables only.

Serves as the testing and optimization sandbox for strategy refinement.

Live Execution Mode

Mirrors the paper mode logic one-for-one but connects to the live Kraken order endpoints.

Uses actual balances and guardrails_v2 enforcement.

Includes trade confirmation, order status polling, and real-time execution feedback.

Runs only when explicitly activated; otherwise dormant.

Each mode will have its own queue/timer schedule and its own storage namespace, ensuring no overlap in data or API activity.
Only one execution engine (paper or live) should ever make Kraken calls at a time.
Passive Learning remains always-on but read-only.

🔗 Phase 3 – Orchestrator / Mode Registry Integration
After the three engines are built and tested individually, we’ll implement a centralized Mode Registry Service to coordinate them.
The registry will:

Maintain the active/inactive status of each mode.

Route data and task scheduling only to active engines.

Expose a unified API for checking system health, mode status, and guardrail states.

Prevent concurrent live + paper execution.

This ensures complete isolation of responsibilities while keeping one coherent control plane.

🧱 Phase 4 – Validation & Regression Testing
Once all modes are live:

Run 48-hour paper-mode tests (as before) to confirm stability.

Compare passive learning logs and paper execution outputs to verify data parity.

Execute a live dry-run with guardrails in monitor-only mode.

Finalize architecture diagrams and SSOT documentation.

📊 Phase 5 – Ongoing Optimization and Feature Refit
After the three-mode system is stable:

Reinstate reporting, analytics, and dashboard aggregation via shared read-only services.

Gradually reintroduce automation (strategy triggers, alerting, etc.) through the Mode Registry scheduler.

Optimize scanning cadence per mode for Kraken API efficiency and real-time performance.

  for m in "${MODES[@]}"; do
    echo "Testing explicit mode=$m for $e"

/**
 * Paper Mode Validation Test (Playwright)
 * ---------------------------------------
 * Automates full paper-trading validation using the frontend UI toggle,
 * while logging backend sync data into /logs/observations/*.csv.
 *
 * Version: v2.0.0-beta-paper-playwright
 * Author: InsightRaCVS Validation Suite
 */

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'fs';
import path from 'path';

// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
// CONFIGURATION
// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
const BASE_URL = process.env.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:5000';
const CSV_DIR = path.join('logs', 'observations');
const RUNTIME_MINUTES = 120; // 2-hour full test max
const SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL_SEC = 600; // Screenshot every 10 minutes
const POLL_INTERVAL_SEC = 30; // CSV observation interval
const PORTFOLIO_INCREMENT = 5; // $5 added per restart (if restart triggered)

// Ensure directory exists
fs.mkdirSync(CSV_DIR, { recursive: true });

// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
// UTILITIES
// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function fetchJSON(endpoint: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE_URL}${endpoint}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Failed to fetch ${endpoint}: ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

function writeCsvHeader(filePath: string) {
  const header =
    'TimestampUTC,Cycle,Tab,BackendEvaluated,BackendEligible,ReadyToBuy,ActiveTrades,Executed,Expired,PassiveLearning,FastLaneSec,TierB,PortfolioValue,WSdeltaMS,UISyncDriftMS\n';
  fs.writeFileSync(filePath, header);
}

function appendCsvRow(filePath: string, data: Record<string, any>) {
  const row = [
    new Date().toISOString(),
    data.cycle,
    data.tab,
    data.backend.evaluated ?? '',
    data.backend.eligible ?? '',
    data.backend.readyToBuy ?? '',
    data.backend.activeTrades ?? '',
    data.backend.executed ?? '',
    data.backend.expired ?? '',
    data.flags.passiveLearning,
    data.timers.fastLane ?? '',
    data.timers.tierB ?? '',
    data.portfolioValue ?? '',
    data.wsDelta ?? '',
    data.uiDrift ?? ''
  ].join(',') + '\n';
  fs.appendFileSync(filePath, row);
}

// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
// MAIN TEST
// ────────────────────────────────────────────────
test.describe('Paper Mode Trading Validation', () => {
  test('runs full trading cycle and logs observations', async ({ page }) => {
    const csvFile = path.join(
      CSV_DIR,
      `paper_mode_observation_${new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:.]/g, '-')}.csv`
    );
    writeCsvHeader(csvFile);

    // Step 1: Launch dashboard
    console.log('🟢 Launching dashboard...');
    await page.goto(BASE_URL);
    await page.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

    // Step 2: Locate Paper Mode toggle and activate
    console.log('🟢 Starting Paper Trading...');
    const toggle = page.locator('text=Paper Trading').first();
    await expect(toggle).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15000 });
    await toggle.click();

    // Verify engine started
    await page.waitForTimeout(8000);
    const config = await fetchJSON('/api/system/config');
    expect(config.systemFlags.isEngineActivePaper).toBe(true);
    expect(config.systemFlags.passiveLearning).toBe(false);

    // Step 3: Begin periodic observation logging
    console.log('📊 Beginning observation logging...');
    const startTime = Date.now();
    let cycle = 0;

    while ((Date.now() - startTime) / 60000 < RUNTIME_MINUTES) {
      cycle++;
      const [summary, metrics] = await Promise.all([
        fetchJSON('/api/trading/summary'),
        fetchJSON('/api/scan/metrics')
      ]);

      const rowData = {
        cycle,
        tab: 'Filter Insights',
        backend: {
          evaluated: summary.evaluated,
          eligible: summary.eligible,
          readyToBuy: summary.readyToBuy,
          activeTrades: summary.executed,
          executed: summary.executed,
          expired: summary.expired
        },
        flags: {
          passiveLearning: config.systemFlags.passiveLearning
        },
        timers: {
          fastLane: metrics.fastLane?.nextInSec ?? '',
          tierB: metrics.tierB?.universeCompleteInSec
            ? `${Math.floor(metrics.tierB.universeCompleteInSec / 60)
                .toString()
                .padStart(2, '0')}:${(metrics.tierB.universeCompleteInSec % 60)
                .toString()
                .padStart(2, '0')}`
            : ''
        },
        portfolioValue: config.systemFlags.portfolioValue ?? '',
        wsDelta: metrics.wsDelta ?? 0,
        uiDrift: metrics.uiDrift ?? 0
      };

      appendCsvRow(csvFile, rowData);

      // Every 10 minutes, capture screenshot
      if (cycle % (SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL_SEC / POLL_INTERVAL_SEC) === 0) {
        const shot = path.join(
          CSV_DIR,
          `snapshot_cycle_${cycle}_${new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:.]/g, '-')}.png`
        );
        await page.screenshot({ path: shot, fullPage: true });
      }

      await page.waitForTimeout(POLL_INTERVAL_SEC * 1000);
    }

    // Step 4: Stop Paper Trading
    console.log('🛑 Stopping Paper Trading...');
    await toggle.click();
    await page.waitForTimeout(5000);

    const stopConfig = await fetchJSON('/api/system/config');
    expect(stopConfig.systemFlags.passiveLearning).toBe(true);
    expect(stopConfig.systemFlags.isEngineActivePaper).toBe(false);

    console.log('✅ Paper Mode Test Completed Successfully.');
    console.log(`CSV Log: ${csvFile}`);
  });
});
🧩 How It Works
Function	Description
fetchJSON()	Reads live backend data from /api endpoints.
writeCsvHeader()	Creates the CSV header structure.
appendCsvRow()	Logs every observation tick (backend + UI state).
Playwright Test Loop	Runs for 1–2 hours, appending every 30 seconds.
page.screenshot()	Captures a full UI snapshot every 10 minutes.
passiveLearning verification	Ensures the backend enters learning mode after stop.
📁 Output Files
Stored under /logs/observations/:

paper_mode_observation_<timestamp>.csv

snapshot_cycle_<n>_<timestamp>.png

Start_application_<timestamp>.log (backend companion)

🧠 Run Command
From your Replit shell:

npx playwright test tests/paper-mode-validation.spec.ts --project=chromium
Or, if you want to run headless (for continuous background validation):

npx playwright test tests/paper-mode-validation.spec.ts --project=chromium --headless
🧾 Restart Handling
When restarting after a fix:

Stop the engine manually (Paper Mode toggle OFF).

Increment portfolio baseline by +$5 before next Playwright run.

Confirm /api/system/config reflects updated portfolio value.

Start Playwright again — the script will automatically log the new baseline.

npx playwright test --list
and confirm paper-mode-validation.spec.ts appears in the test list.

function safeArray(val: unknown): string[] {
  if (Array.isArray(val)) return val.filter(x => typeof x === "string");

⚠️ 1. The Real Risks of Refactoring the Trading Engine Startup
A well-done refactor can make the system simpler and faster, but because the trading engine is at the core of everything (portfolio management, scanner triggers, passive learning), there are a few specific risk zones to manage.

🔹 a. State-management side effects
If we change when and how the trading state flips from “stopped” → “active,” we have to make sure every subsystem (scanner, portfolio manager, goals engine) listens to the same new signal.
Otherwise, you could briefly get:

The scanner thinking trading is on while the execution engine isn’t ready

The portfolio updating too early or skipping its first balance snapshot

WebSocket clients showing mixed states for a few seconds

➡️ Mitigation: clearly define a single “authoritative event” (e.g., engine_start_confirmed) and make all modules subscribe to that.

🔹 b. Race conditions with asynchronous tasks
The engine currently relies on a chain of awaited async calls that ensure order (e.g., “create portfolio → start engine → send broadcast”).
Flattening those calls into an instant-ACK model can re-introduce race conditions if not carefully guarded.

➡️ Mitigation: wrap the sequence in a lightweight state machine or queue (e.g., state = STARTING → RUNNING → STOPPING → STOPPED) so only one transition runs at a time.

🔹 c. Historical data integrity
Portfolio balance, trade history, and learning logs all depend on timestamps.
If we change when “start” officially happens, it could create gaps or overlaps in session data.

➡️ Mitigation: mark every new session with an ack timestamp and an activation timestamp so both user-facing and analytic systems stay consistent.

🔹 d. WebSocket event compatibility
Your current WebSocket payloads (trading_state_changed, trading_state_ack, etc.) are consumed not only by the UI but also by background jobs (e.g., scanner cadence, telemetry).
Renaming or reordering them can break listeners silently.

➡️ Mitigation: preserve the existing event types; add new ones alongside (e.g., engine_start_ack) rather than replacing the old ones until the whole stack is migrated.

🔹 e. Regression risk in live-mode trading (future)
When you eventually introduce real live trading, timing precision becomes more critical.
Any hidden delays or out-of-order messages could have financial impact.

Now that the trading engine and market scanner are stable and synchronized, we’ll address one of the few remaining structural bottlenecks: the engine startup sequence.
Currently, pressing the Trading Toggle sends a REST request that passes through multiple async layers before the UI reflects the “Active” state.
This creates a ~30–40 second visual lag even though the engine technically starts almost immediately.

This refactor aims to flatten and modernize that startup chain — replacing the chained async workflow with a single, event-driven architecture that gives instant feedback to the user while maintaining full backend integrity.

🎯 Objectives
Eliminate 30–40s startup delay
Trading state, portfolio updates, and passive learning indicators should appear within <1s of the toggle being pressed.

Implement real-time acknowledgements (ACKs)
Frontend receives a WebSocket engine_start_ack event as soon as the backend accepts the command, providing immediate UI feedback.

Simplify backend flow
Replace the current multi-promise chain (HTTP → service → sync → DB → broadcast) with a direct ack → confirm → reconcile lifecycle.

Future-proof the architecture
Establish a unified, state-driven design that works identically for paper and live trading modes.

🧩 Implementation Overview
Backend Changes
Introduce a real-time command channel for start/stop actions (WebSocket or lightweight RPC).

Refactor paper-sim-service.ts and trading-state-sync.ts to:

Separate command acknowledgement from engine initialization.

Send an immediate engine_start_ack or engine_stop_ack broadcast (within <100 ms).

Continue DB writes and initialization asynchronously.

Add a state machine (STOPPED → STARTING → RUNNING → STOPPING) to serialize transitions and eliminate race conditions.

Preserve backward-compatibility: existing REST endpoints remain functional, but internally route through the new state machine.

Frontend Changes
Update toggle button handler in useTrading.tsx:

Send command via WebSocket instead of REST.

Update UI state immediately upon ACK receipt.

Confirm with engine_start_confirmed or engine_stop_confirmed messages.

Remove reliance on 10s or 15s React Query polling for trading status.

Maintain portfolio balance hydration via the same ACK payload.

Logging & Diagnostics
Log full lifecycle timestamps for every session start/stop:

[StartupRefactor] user=<id> ack=<ts> confirm=<ts> reconcile=<ts> latency=<ms>
Add a safety timeout (e.g., 5 s) — if confirmation never arrives, revert UI to “Stopped” and log a warning.

🧠 Risk Mitigation
Risk	Mitigation
State desync (e.g., engine active but UI inactive)	Centralized state machine controls all transitions
Race conditions from concurrent starts/stops	Queue start/stop commands, enforce serialized state transitions
Breaking scanner or passive learning flows	Keep old WebSocket event names and add new ones alongside (engine_start_ack, engine_start_confirmed)
Data-integrity drift in portfolio or session history	Maintain both ackTimestamp and activationTimestamp in DB records
UI regressions	Feature-flag the new flow for test users before global rollout
⚙️ Optional Adjacent Cleanups
If you’re refactoring this area, it’s efficient to tidy up nearby modules at the same time:

PortfolioManager – switch from periodic DB polling to event-driven balance updates.

Execution Queue – replace chained promises with a small job queue (retry + timeout).

Session Lifecycle – consolidate start/stop logic from multiple files into one controller.

Scanner Bridge – stream scan_tick data directly to the engine rather than through cache.

Logging System – unify backend logs into structured JSON for long-term latency tracking.

🧪 Testing Plan

password: SecurePass123!

Verify portfolio balance updates instantly.

Ensure scanner and passive learning indicators switch correctly and stay in sync.

🧩 Expected Outcomes
Area	Before	After
UI reaction time	30–40 s	< 1 s
Architecture	Chained async promises	Flat event-driven flow
Debugging	Hard to trace	Single unified state log
Reliability	Occasional race conditions	Deterministic lifecycle
Future extension	Paper-only	Paper + Live compatible
🔒 Rollback Plan
If the refactor introduces instability:

Toggle a config flag USE_NEW_ENGINE_STARTUP=false in .env

Revert to the existing REST-based sequence instantly

Logs remain available for comparison and rollback analysis

🏁 Summary
This refactor isn’t just a UX polish.
It’s a structural modernization of the trading engine startup, eliminating lag, clarifying state transitions, and preparing the system for future live trading support — while keeping full backward compatibility and safety fallbacks.

1. What does LSP stand for?
LSP = Language Server Protocol

It’s the system that powers:

IntelliSense auto-completion

TypeScript static analysis

Real-time error detection

Code linting

Type hinting and symbol resolution

Unused variables

Code referencing removed options (“learning”)

Mismatched shapes between server and client

These existed before refactor, and Replit did not fix them because we instructed them not to touch business logic yet.

(B) Runtime-only paths that TypeScript can’t infer
Some code paths load dynamic maps, dynamic JSON, or dynamic keys that TypeScript can’t verify.

(C) Typescript complaining about files that are basically “junk drawers”
Large files like server/routes.ts (6,000+ lines) often contain:

Unused legacy code

Mixed type declarations

Copy/paste blocks

Dead endpoints

Old diagnostic code

We will be cleaning these up in Phase 6.

**The Strategy Engine is the source of truth.

Strategy Engine → consumes those real results to generate signals

ReadyToBuy engine → consumes Strategy Engine outputs

UI → purely renders what the engine outputs

Phase 6 ensures this pipeline is correct, synchronized, and consistent.

🎯 PHASE 6 OBJECTIVE — Strategy Engine Alignment Refactor
Fix, normalize, and align the Strategy Engine so that:

It receives correct inputs from the MarketScanner and filters.

Its outputs (signals) are authoritative and sent downstream to ReadyToBuy and UI.

All strategies apply decisions based on the true filtered universe, not UI-driven values.

All strategy outputs are consistent, synchronized, and based on the same versioned cycle.

Historical strategy code, unused paths, and legacy behaviors do not influence results.

This is a plumbing-alignment refactor, not a rewrite of strategy logic or parameters.
Do NOT change any business rules, thresholds, or strategy math.

🔧 PHASE 6 — REQUIRED IMPLEMENTATION TASKS
Task 1 — Fix Strategy Engine Inputs
Ensure the Strategy Engine receives only the following authoritative inputs:

eligibleSymbols[] from ScanTickContext (current cycle)

Fully-filtered strategy prerequisites (candles, OHLCV, indicators, etc.)

Current trading mode (paper or live)

Current passiveLearning flag

Current stateVersion (from scan_tick)

Reject and warn if:

UI-provided values attempt to influence strategy computation

Legacy endpoints provide inconsistent or stale data

Symbols not present in eligibleSymbols[] are passed to the engine

The Strategy Engine must run only on the authoritative eligibleSymbols array.

Task 2 — Align All Strategies to the Unified Input Model
Each strategy must follow the same input structure:

StrategyInput {
  symbol: string
  candles: Candle[]
  indicators: IndicatorSet
  meta: {
    mode: "paper" | "live",
    passiveLearning: boolean,
    scanCycleId: string,
    stateVersion: number
  }
}
If any strategy expects different fields or naming conventions, normalize them.

Do NOT change strategy logic — only ensure consistent, correct inputs.

Task 3 — Centralize Strategy Invocation
Move all strategy invocation logic into the existing
SignalGenerationCoordinator (created in Phase 5).

Coordinator responsibilities:

Receive eligibleSymbols[]

Fetch prerequisites once (shared cache)

Run all strategies with concurrency controls

Capture performance metrics

Produce final GeneratedSignal[] output

This ensures identical inputs for all strategies.

Task 4 — Establish Version Gating & Cycle Synchronization
For each cycle:

Receive scan_tick (v=N)

Compute strategy signals using version N

Cache results under version N

broadcast ready_to_buy with version N

Reject any strategy results computed for older versions

This prevents:

Race conditions

Out-of-order strategy results

Strategies being executed twice for the same cycle

UI seeing mismatched signal sets

Task 5 — Public API Normalization
Update any strategy-related REST endpoints to always return:

mode

passiveLearning

scanCycleId

stateVersion

eligibleSymbols[]

signals[]

If an endpoint returns:

different field names

missing fields

stale or cached values not tied to the current cycle

→ fix it.

Task 6 — Cleanup & Remove Legacy Strategy Paths
Inside StrategyEngine and related files, identify and remove:

Old v1/v2 strategy paths

Duplicated implementations

Unused helper functions

Unreachable branches

Strategy logic that used old API responses

Console logs from abandoned code

This cleanup should not change strategy behavior — only remove dead or misleading code.

Manual test cycles

Playwright tests (same as Phase 4/5)

Short answer:

Yes, the earlier “refactor” did touch the trading engine, but mostly around the edges (status, timers, sync), not the core plumbing.

It wasn’t enough because you still had two data paths, two “truths,” and a half-removed v2 living alongside the original engine.

There are other parts of the app worth a hard look if the goal is “grow the portfolio as much as possible, as fast as possible, inside our risk rules.”

I’ll break that down in plain language.

1. What we really did in the earlier refactor — and why it wasn’t enough
When you abandoned “v2” and went back to the original engine, what actually happened (based on the files/logs Replit and I have been working through) was roughly this:

What v2 tried to do
V2 introduced things like:

A new mode (learning) in addition to paper and live

New APIs and WebSocket message types

Extra diagnostic endpoints (like /api/filters/diagnostics)

New ways of computing / presenting counts and states

But it never fully replaced v1. Instead, you ended up with:

v1 engine logic still running

v2-style events & endpoints coexisting

UI bits wired to a weird mixture of both

So instead of “v2 replacing v1”, you had:

Hybrid Frankenstein version: old engine + new concepts + partial cleanup.

What the “back to original + refactor” phase actually changed
That earlier refactor (before the Stage 3 plan we’re doing now) mainly did things like:

Try to improve synchronization between backend and UI:

Start/stop trading indicators

Countdown timer for scans

TopBar and dashboard showing “ACTIVE / STOPPED / PASSIVE LEARNING”

Add reconciliation logic:

Version numbers on trading_state events

Reject obviously old/bad state updates

Tweak polling intervals and WebSocket behavior:

Less polling, more socket-driven updates

Some retry logic for WebSocket delivery

And it sort of helped:

Fewer cases where the UI was completely lying

Less “stuck at 0 seconds”

Better consistency in some states

But it didn’t fix the core architectural problems, specifically:

Two sources of truth

One path using scan_tick & real engine state

Another path using 24h diagnostics or legacy endpoints

UI components mixing these arbitrarily (Filter Health vs Filter Insights vs Filtered Pairs showing different counts)

Mode confusion (learning vs paper)

“Learning” introduced as an actual mode instead of “paper + passiveLearning=true”

Scanner ran in “learning” while UI asked for mode=paper → 404s, mismatches, or stale data

Some logic computed passiveLearning = !isActive, some didn’t

Legacy code paths still active

Duplicate /scan/state endpoints

Legacy scan_tick format still emitted

Legacy scan consumers still listening in places

Portions of v2 still influencing results even though conceptually you “went back” to v1

Scanner & history coupling was wrong

Scanner waiting on history/heartbeat from engines that weren’t running

Long blocking loops (70+ pairs history checks)

Result: scans hanging or taking forever, no timely data for strategies

So the refactor you did back then was:

“Let’s try to make this hybrid behave better”
instead of
“Let’s simplify to one clean pipeline with a single source of truth.”

That’s why it was never fully satisfying and why we had to do the deeper Stage 3 work now.

2. What’s different about the current refactor (why this is “doing it properly”)
The Stage 3 work (Phases 0–5, and upcoming 6–7) is fundamentally different in character:

Single Source of Truth (SSOT)

Trading state & scanner state are versioned, cached, broadcast once

scan_tick & trading_state_changed are the canonical events

Diagnostics / 24h widgets are explicitly labeled as “Last 24h”, not mixed into live state

Normalized modes

Only mode: "paper" | "live"

Learning is no longer a “mode” — it’s mode: "paper" + passiveLearning: true

We normalized API responses and WS payloads so everything sees paper / live consistently

ScanTickProvider & TradingModeProvider at the app root

WS events are processed once, centrally

Components just read these contexts via hooks (useScanTick, useTradingMode)

No more “this tab wasn’t mounted so it missed the events”

Ready-to-Buy & Strategy coordination

ReadyToBuy engine runs after scan_tick for the same cycle/version

Uses only eligibleSymbols from the scanner, not some random UI count

SignalGenerationCoordinator centralizes strategy invocation with concurrency, caching, instrumentation

This is the “plumbing refactor” the earlier pass never attempted.

3. Other areas we should consider refactoring (beyond what we’re already doing)
You said:

Nothing is off the table. The goal is to grow the portfolio as much as possible, as fast as possible, within risk parameters.

With that goal, these are the other areas I’d take a hard look at once Phases 6–7 of the trading pipeline are done. I’ll mark them by impact and risk to core goal.

A. Portfolio & PnL Engine
(High impact, medium refactor cost)

Questions I’d want answered (via code + logs):

How are realized / unrealized PnL calculated?

Does the portfolio aggregator correctly handle:

Partial fills

Multiple entries / exits in same symbol

Fees

Multi-currency (if applicable)

Are the dashboard widgets all reading from a single, authoritative portfolio snapshot? Or are there multiple differently-aggregated views?

Why this matters for you:

If PnL / portfolio math is even a bit off, the system can look like it’s “growing” but actually isn’t — or vice versa. For a “grow as much as possible, as fast as possible” goal, this is critical truth infrastructure.

B. Risk / Sizing / Exposure logic
(Very high impact, depends on how much exists today)

You want fast growth inside risk boundaries. So we should inspect:

Position sizing logic:

% of equity per trade

Max concurrent positions

Per-symbol caps

Sector / correlation caps (if any)

Stop/risk handling:

Does the system even know where the “risk point” is for each trade?

Is it enforcing that at size-time, or only in backtest?

If risk rules exist only in documentation or in a half-used config structure, we should consider a small risk-engine refactor so:

Strategy says “I like this symbol” → risk engine says “how much can we responsibly buy?” → execution engine does exactly that.

Right now, most of our work has been about timing and correctness, not risk math.

C. Execution & Simulation flow (paper and live)
(High impact on realism, medium complexity)

Files we’ve already seen hints of:

paper-execution-engine.ts

paper-sim-service.ts

paper-execution.ts

kraken.ts (or other exchange adapters)

Key questions:

Is paper execution simulating realistic fills (slippage, partial fills, delays), or just “price at bar close”?

Does live mode share as much code as possible with paper mode? Or are there two divergent paths?

Are there race conditions where:

A signal is generated

UI displays it

But execution never actually happens or the portfolio never updates?

For your goal, this is crucial:

If signals are excellent but the execution layer is flaky, portfolio growth will underperform what the strategy is capable of.

D. Goals / LATTI / Parameter Engine
(Medium–high impact, sensitive area)

You’ve been clear:

LATTI and the goals/parameter engine define what the system is trying to achieve and what risk boundaries exist.

You’d rather not change LATTI unless absolutely necessary.

What I recommend:

Short audit, not deep refactor yet:

Verify that the parameters LATTI writes (goals, risk, constraints) are being read correctly by:

Strategy engine

Risk/position sizing

Scanner (if it uses ranges/whitelists)

Confirm there are no “shadow configs” (hard-coded overrides bypassing LATTI).

If we later discover “LATTI says X, engine does Y”, then we plan a targeted refactor. But we don’t start there.

E. Trade History, Reporting, and Analytics
(Medium impact, high value for trust and tuning)

Even if the engine trades perfectly, you need:

Solid trade history (all fills, timestamps, prices, PnL).

Good performance analytics:

Win rate

Expectancy per trade

Max drawdown

Equity curve over time

Per-strategy attribution (“which strategies are actually making money?”)

We’ve seen hints of DB issues in logs (e.g., malformed array literals, alignment-verifier, reflective-intelligence). Those may not directly break trading, but they can:

Slow down the system

Pollute logs

Make debugging miserable

Hide insights needed to tune strategies and risk configs

Given your growth goal, I’d want this stack solid too — so we can measure what the engine is really doing.

F. routes.ts & Monolithic API surface
(Medium risk, necessary long term)

You’ve heard this theme:

server/routes.ts is big, has pre-existing TypeScript diagnostics, and multiple duplicate definitions (like /scan/state pre-fix).

Over time, this kind of monolith becomes:

Hard to reason about

Easy to break when adding new endpoints

A source of subtle bugs (incorrect handler being used, auth applied inconsistently)

I wouldn’t start a “routes.ts redesign” until:

The trading pipeline refactor is fully done (Phases 6–7).

We have a clear picture of which endpoints are hot-path, which are legacy, which can be retired.

But in a “nothing off the table” mindset, yes: this is a prime candidate for modularization once the core engine is stable.

4. How I’d approach “refactor properly” from here
If we zoom out:

Stage 3 / Phases 0–6 → Repair & normalize the trading pipeline

Then, in order of importance to your goal:

Verify & harden Portfolio + PnL engine

Audit & align Risk/sizing logic with your risk parameters

Harden execution simulation and live path

Check that LATTI/Goals parameters are actually honored

Stabilize trade history + analytics + performance reports

Gradually modularize routes.ts and clean up remaining legacy code paths

That order keeps us tightly aligned with your core objective:

✅ “Make the system genuinely capable of growing the portfolio aggressively
🔒 but inside the risk constraints we define.”

And we do it without casually rewriting everything or changing the intent of what you’ve already designed — we just keep uncovering and fixing the plumbing until the behavior matches the design.

If you’d like, next step I can:

Propose a post-Phase-7 audit plan listing exactly which files to inspect in each area (Portfolio, Risk, Execution, etc.), in the same style we used for the scanner/trading engine, so we can keep going deliberately instead of randomly poking at things.

Data wiring:

  - eligibleThisScan  = scan_tick.eligible (or equivalent field)
  - ineligibleThisScan = max(0, evaluatedThisScan - eligibleThisScan)

Semantics:
  - evaluatedThisScan should be ≈ 60 in the normal paper engine run.

  3) Total Survived Filters (24h)
     - All filter passes (times a symbol passed all filters) over 24h.

3️⃣ Clarifying the “2–3 Second” Fresh-Data Idea vs 30-Second Scans
You’re right to flag this — there are two different concepts:

Universe scan

Every 30 seconds, ~60 pairs are scanned.

These 60 are split between:

Top 100 “priority” universe (so each of those gets hit about once per minute).

The remaining long tail (cycled over ~10–15 minutes).

This is what feeds the filters and the rolling filtered pool.

Per-symbol price refresh for strategy / open trades / RTB (what I hinted at for Phase 9)

Idea: have faster price updates (e.g., 2–3 seconds) but only for:

Symbols in the Active Filtered Pool

Symbols currently in Ready-to-Buy

Symbols in Open Trades

The important clarification:

Those 2–3 second refreshes do NOT have to go through the 60-symbol / 30-second scan pipe.

For Phase 9, the architecture I have in mind is:

Keep the full-universe scanner exactly as-is:

60 symbols / 30 seconds

Rotation logic: Top 100 every minute, full 1,530 in ~10–15 minutes

Add a separate “lightweight price feed” layer:

Pulls only prices (and maybe 24h vol) for a small set:

Active Filtered Pool

Ready-to-Buy symbols

Open Trade symbols

Uses either:

A Kraken websocket price stream, or

A small REST call batch within Kraken rate limits

Updated every 2–3 seconds, but on a tiny symbol set (dozens, not thousands).

So:

We do not “eat into” the 60-symbol budget used for universe scanning.

We do not slow down the universe rotation.

We do give strategies, RTB, and open trades much fresher pricing.

We can lock this design in more concretely when we write the Phase 9 directive, but the key promise:

The 2–3 second updates will be a separate, lightweight pricing feed for a small subset,
not an expansion of the main 60-per-30s scan.

Once you’ve had a chance to test the new version, we can then move into the Phase 9 design for fresh-data flows and strategy evaluation timing.

Total Survived Filters (24h) → rolling sum of all eligible survivors (duplicates allowed).

1. Dawn Trader – Purpose & Objective
Dawn Trader is an automated trading system for the crypto market (currently Kraken spot).

Use a set of predefined + evolving strategies to grow the portfolio balance as much and as fast as reasonably possible, while staying strictly inside the risk limits you define.

Key points:

Trading modes:

Paper (simulated) – where all refactoring & testing happens first

Live (real orders) – to be implemented after the pipeline is proven in paper

Risk is controlled via the Core Four Guardrails:

portfolio_risk_per_trade_pct (e.g. 4%) – max % of portfolio you are allowed to risk on any one trade

symbol_cooldown_minutes – how long a symbol must “rest” after a completed trade before being traded again

max_open_positions – max number of concurrent trades

daily_loss_kill_switch_pct / kill_switch_triggered – if daily loss exceeds threshold, shut trading down

The system is built to allow AI-assisted evolution: filters, guardrails, and strategies can be adjusted over time by LATTΙ and, later, by a rebuilt Walter.

3. High-Level System Architecture (Current)
Conceptually, the system has these major pipelines:

Market Data Ingestion

Periodic scan of Kraken’s pairs universe (currently ~1530 pairs).

Every 30 seconds, the system selects a batch of ~60 symbols:

Some from Top 100 universe

Some from non-Top-100 universe

This creates a scan cycle identified by a cycleId like:
cycle_paper_8tjSNY_kB0

Emits a scan_tick event with:

mode (paper/live)

cadenceMs (30,000 ms)

evaluated and eligible counts

a stateVersion (version gating)

eligibleSymbols list, etc.

Filter Pipeline

New pairs from each scan go through a multi-stage filter system:

Liquidity thresholds (24h volume, etc.)

Spread / slippage

Exchange-specific constraints

Cooldowns & dedup logic

Output:

Per-cycle view: how many evaluated, how many passed filters (eligible), how many failed filters (ineligible).

A rolling filtered pool (deduped, TTL-based) of all currently active filtered pairs (non-expired, deduped).

Strategy Pipeline

For each eligible pair (from the filtered pool), a subset of strategies are applied:

Historically: up to 9 strategies, but only the top 2–3 per symbol based on a ranking/priority system.

Strategies compute:

Entry price

Stop loss

Target / take-profit

Confidence

Context metrics (VWAP, range %, etc.)

Output:

Ready-to-buy signals (sub-set of eligible pairs that meet strategy rules).

Ready-To-Buy (RTB) & State Cache

Strategy results are aggregated into a ReadyToBuy payload.

This is broadcast through ContextBridge / WebSockets to:

The UI (Ready-to-Buy table)

The Trading Engine subscriber side (ReadyToBuySubscriber)

A State Cache (Stage 3) stores the latest snapshot, with versioning & gating.

Trading Engine (Paper mode currently)

ReadyToBuySubscriber receives signals and forwards them to:

PaperPortfolioManager, which coordinates:

Risk management

Position sizing (using portfolio_risk_per_trade_pct and portfolio metrics)

Cooldowns & maxOpenPositions

The RiskManager enforces Core Four guardrails.

If all checks pass, the Paper Execution Engine simulates:

Order placement

Fills

P&L update

Portfolio metrics updates (cash, holdings, total value)

UI Surfaces

Filter Insights tab

Shows scan & filter status: cycle, counts, 24h stats, filtered pool list, filter breakdown.

Ready To Buy tab

Shows strategy signals (symbol, strategy, entry, stop, target, VWAP, volume, etc.).

Open Trades / Positions tab

Shows active positions in paper trading (and later in live mode).

9. Architectural Invariants & Pitfalls
Invariants
Single source of truth per concern:

Only one place defines what a “filtered pool” is.

Only one RiskManager controls risk decisions.

Only one pipeline from scan_tick → ready_to_buy → TradingEngine.

No hidden guardrails

All limits must be visible in guardrails_v2 or clearly documented.

No magic percentages like 10% or 25% baked into code.

Fail-fast over silent defaults

If data is missing or invalid:

Throw/log clearly

Reject the trade / event, don’t silently proceed with fake defaults.

Event-driven, version-gated flows

Avoid direct “ad hoc” calling patterns bypassing the event system.

Use stateVersion + cycleId to avoid stale data.

Replit sometimes:

Implements layout but ignores semantics.

Adds new columns/fields to DB or schema unilaterally (e.g. max_position_size_pct).

Introduces new “safety” rules that violate your design (extra caps, extra guardrails).

Alignment Verifier Code:
import { db } from '../db'; 
import { alignmentPolicies, alignmentAuditLog, goalAlignmentProfile } from '@shared/schema'; 
import { eq, and, desc } from 'drizzle-orm'; 
import { nanoid } from 'nanoid'; 
import type { contextBridge as ContextBridgeType } from './context-bridge'; 
/** 
* AlignmentVerifier - Pre-Execution Alignment Validation 
* 
* Purpose: Ensures all autonomous actions align with system objectives and policies 
* before execution, providing a safety gate for AI-driven decisions. 
* 
* Features: 
* - Policy-based action validation 
* - Risk constraint checking 
* - Alignment score computation 
* - Audit trail logging 
*/ 
export class AlignmentVerifier { 
constructor(private contextBridge: typeof ContextBridgeType) {} 
/** 
* Verify an action against alignment policies 
*/ 
async verifyAction(params: { 
actionType: string; 
actionParams: Record<string, any>; 
policyType: string; 
requestedBy: string; 
mode?: 'live' | 'paper'; 
}): Promise<{ 
approved: boolean; 
alignmentScore: number; 
rationale: string; 
constraints: string[]; 
warnings: string[]; 
}> { 
const { actionType, actionParams, policyType, requestedBy, mode } = params; 
const auditId = audit-${nanoid()}; 
console.log([AlignmentVerifier] 🔍 Verifying action: ${actionType} (type: ${policyType})); 
try { 
// 1. Load active policies for this type 
const policies = await db 
.select() 
.from(alignmentPolicies) 
.where( 
and( 
eq(alignmentPolicies.isActive, true), 
eq(alignmentPolicies.policyType, policyType as any) 
) 
); 
if (policies.length === 0) { 
console.warn([AlignmentVerifier] ⚠️ No active policies found for type: ${policyType}); 
} 
// 2. Load current alignment profile (initialize if missing) 
let profile = await db 
.select() 
.from(goalAlignmentProfile) 
.orderBy(desc(goalAlignmentProfile.updatedAt)) 
.limit(1) 
.then((rows: any[]) => rows[0]); 
// Initialize profile if it doesn't exist 
if (!profile) { 
console.log("[AlignmentVerifier] ⚠️ No profile found, initializing default profile..."); 
const { AdaptiveObjectiveEngine } = await import('./adaptive-objective-engine'); 
const adaptiveEngine = new AdaptiveObjectiveEngine(this.contextBridge); 
profile = await adaptiveEngine.initializeProfile(); 
} 
// 3. Evaluate action against policies 
const evaluation = this.evaluateAgainstPolicies( 
actionType, 
actionParams, 
policies, 
profile 
); 
// 4. Compute alignment score 
const alignmentScore = this.computeAlignmentScore(evaluation, profile); 
// 5. Determine approval 
const approved = alignmentScore >= 0.6 && evaluation.violations.length === 0; 
// 6. Generate rationale 
const rationale = this.generateRationale( 
approved, 
alignmentScore, 
evaluation, 
policies 
); 
// 7. Log audit trail 
await db.insert(alignmentAuditLog).values({ 
auditId, 
timestamp: new Date(), 
verificationResult: approved ? 'approved' : 'rejected', 
proposedChange: { 
actionType, 
actionParams, 
requestedBy 
}, 
violatedPolicies: evaluation.violations, 
alignmentScore, 
recommendations: evaluation.warnings, 
metadata: { 
policyType, 
appliedPolicies: policies.map((p: any) => p.policyId), 
constraints: evaluation.constraints 
} 
}); 
console.log( 
[AlignmentVerifier] ${approved ? '✅' : '❌'} Verification ${approved ? 'PASSED' : 'FAILED'} - Score: ${alignmentScore.toFixed(2)} 
); 
// 8. Broadcast verification result 
await this.contextBridge.broadcast({ 
type: "state_update", 
userId: null, // System-level event 
mode: mode, // Include mode if provided (user-initiated) or undefined (autonomous) 
payload: { 
eventType: "alignment_verification_complete", 
auditId, 
actionType, 
approved, 
alignmentScore, 
rationale 
} 
}); 
return { 
approved, 
alignmentScore, 
rationale, 
constraints: evaluation.constraints, 
warnings: evaluation.warnings 
}; 
} catch (error) { 
console.error([AlignmentVerifier] ❌ Verification failed:, error); 
// Log failed verification 
await db.insert(alignmentAuditLog).values({ 
auditId, 
timestamp: new Date(), 
verificationResult: 'flagged', 
proposedChange: { 
actionType, 
actionParams, 
requestedBy 
}, 
violatedPolicies: ['verification_error'], 
alignmentScore: 0, 
recommendations: [Verification error: ${error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Unknown error'}], 
metadata: { error: true } 
}); 
return { 
approved: false, 
alignmentScore: 0, 
rationale: Verification failed due to system error, 
constraints: ['error_state'], 
warnings: ['System in error state - action rejected'] 
}; 
} 
} 
/** 
* Evaluate action against policy constraints 
*/ 
private evaluateAgainstPolicies( 
actionType: string, 
actionParams: Record<string, any>, 
policies: Array<{ 
policyId: string; 
policyType: string; 
constraints: any; 
priority: number; 
}>, 
profile?: { 
objectives: any; 
targetMetrics: any; 
} 
): { 
violations: string[]; 
constraints: string[]; 
warnings: string[]; 
policyMatches: number; 
} { 
const violations: string[] = []; 
const constraints: string[] = []; 
const warnings: string[] = []; 
let policyMatches = 0; 
for (const policy of policies) { 
const policyConstraints = policy.constraints || {}; 
// Check for action type restrictions 
if (policyConstraints.allowedActions && Array.isArray(policyConstraints.allowedActions)) { 
if (!policyConstraints.allowedActions.includes(actionType)) { 
violations.push(action_not_allowed: ${actionType} not in allowed list); 
} else { 
policyMatches++; 
} 
} 
// Check risk limits for trading actions 
if (actionType.includes('trade') || actionType.includes('order')) { 
if (policyConstraints.maxRiskPerTrade && actionParams.amount) { 
const riskAmount = parseFloat(actionParams.amount); 
const maxRisk = parseFloat(policyConstraints.maxRiskPerTrade); 
if (riskAmount > maxRisk) { 
violations.push(risk_exceeded: ${riskAmount} > ${maxRisk}); 
} 
} 
if (policyConstraints.requiredApproval && actionParams.amount) { 
const amount = parseFloat(actionParams.amount); 
const threshold = parseFloat(policyConstraints.requiredApproval.threshold || '1000'); 
if (amount > threshold) { 
warnings.push(manual_approval_required: Amount ${amount} exceeds threshold ${threshold}); 
} 
} 
} 
// Check domain-specific constraints 
if (policyConstraints.domainRules) { 
const rules = policyConstraints.domainRules; 
if (rules.maxActionsPerHour && actionParams.frequency) { 
const freq = parseInt(actionParams.frequency); 
if (freq > rules.maxActionsPerHour) { 
violations.push(frequency_exceeded: ${freq} actions/hour > ${rules.maxActionsPerHour}); 
} 
} 
if (rules.requiresContext && !actionParams.context) { 
warnings.push('context_missing: Action requires contextual justification'); 
} 
} 
// Add policy constraints to list 
if (policyConstraints.mustComplyWith) { 
constraints.push(...policyConstraints.mustComplyWith); 
} 
} 
return { violations, constraints, warnings, policyMatches }; 
} 
/** 
* Compute alignment score (0.0 - 1.0) 
*/ 
private computeAlignmentScore( 
evaluation: { 
violations: string[]; 
warnings: string[]; 
policyMatches: number; 
}, 
profile?: { 
objectives: any; 
} 
): number { 
let score = 1.0; 
// Deduct for violations (severe) 
score -= evaluation.violations.length * 0.3; 
// Deduct for warnings (moderate) 
score -= evaluation.warnings.length * 0.1; 
// Bonus for policy matches 
score += evaluation.policyMatches * 0.05; 
// Weight by profile objectives if available 
if (profile?.objectives) { 
const objectives = profile.objectives; 
if (typeof objectives === 'object' && objectives !== null) { 
const avgObjective = Object.values(objectives).reduce((sum: number, w: any) => sum + (parseFloat(w) || 0), 0) / Object.keys(objectives).length; 
score *= avgObjective; // Scale by average objective weight 
} 
} 
// Clamp to [0, 1] 
return Math.max(0, Math.min(1, score)); 
} 
/** 
* Generate human-readable rationale 
*/ 
private generateRationale( 
approved: boolean, 
alignmentScore: number, 
evaluation: { 
violations: string[]; 
warnings: string[]; 
policyMatches: number; 
}, 
policies: Array<{ policyId: string; policyType: string }> 
): string { 
if (!approved) { 
if (evaluation.violations.length > 0) { 
return Action rejected due to policy violations: ${evaluation.violations.join(', ')}; 
} 
return Action rejected due to low alignment score (${alignmentScore.toFixed(2)} < 0.60); 
} 
const parts: string[] = [ 
Action approved with alignment score ${alignmentScore.toFixed(2)} 
]; 
if (evaluation.policyMatches > 0) { 
parts.push(matched ${evaluation.policyMatches} policies); 
} 
if (evaluation.warnings.length > 0) { 
parts.push(warnings: ${evaluation.warnings.join(', ')}); 
} 
return parts.join('; '); 
}
/** 
* Batch verify multiple actions 
*/ 
async verifyBatch(actions: Array<{ 
actionType: string; 
actionParams: Record<string, any>; 
policyType: string; 
requestedBy: string; 
}>): Promise<Array<{ 
approved: boolean; 
alignmentScore: number; 
rationale: string; 
}>> { 
console.log([AlignmentVerifier] 📦 Batch verifying ${actions.length} actions); 
const results = await Promise.all( 
actions.map(action => this.verifyAction(action)) 
); 
const approvedCount = results.filter(r => r.approved).length; 
console.log([AlignmentVerifier] ✅ Batch complete: ${approvedCount}/${actions.length} approved); 
return results; 
}

async getVerificationHistory(limit: number = 20): Promise<Array<{

alignmentScore: number | null;

verificationResult: alignmentAuditLog.verificationResult, 
proposedChange: alignmentAuditLog.proposedChange, 
alignmentScore: alignmentAuditLog.alignmentScore, 
recommendations: alignmentAuditLog.recommendations 
}) 
.from(alignmentAuditLog) 
.orderBy(desc(alignmentAuditLog.timestamp)) 
.limit(limit); 
return history; 
} 
}
